subject: physics
title: Refraction and Total Internal Reflection
welcome_lead: Bend light at boundaries with Snell's law and trap it inside optical fibres.
meta_desc: A-Level Waves adventure on refractive index, Snell's law and total internal reflection.
final_note: Above the critical angle, no light escapes — that is fibre optics in one sentence.

concepts.def: n = c / v in the medium.
n1 sin theta1 = n2 sin theta2.
Angle giving theta2 = 90°: sin theta_c = n2/n1.
All light reflected when theta > theta_c.
Glass guide using TIR to keep light inside.

walkthroughs.body_html: n = speed of light in vacuum / speed in medium. Always n >= 1. Light slows when entering a denser medium, bending towards the normal.
n1 sin(theta1) = n2 sin(theta2). Travelling into a denser medium (higher n), theta decreases. Into a less dense medium, theta increases.
For light going from denser to less dense (n1 > n2), if theta1 > theta_c where sin(theta_c) = n2/n1, the light fully reflects internally. This traps light in fibres.

mcqs.q: Refractive index of a medium is:
options: v / c
c / v
c × v
c - v

mcqs.q: Total internal reflection requires light travelling:
options: Less dense to denser
Denser to less dense
Through a vacuum
Along the boundary

mcqs.q: What condition must be met for total internal reflection to occur?
options: No — internal energy refers only to the chemical potential energy.
Any angle is fine as long as the light is going into a less dense medium.
Light must travel from a denser to a less dense medium AND strike the boundary at an angle greater than the critical angle.
Light must go from a less dense to a denser medium.

mcqs.q: Why does light bend when it enters a denser medium like glass?
options: Because it slows down — the change in speed at the boundary causes the wavefront to bend (towards the normal).
Because the medium is denser, it physically blocks part of the light and forces it to turn.
No — internal energy refers only to the chemical potential energy.
Because gravity in the glass pulls the light down.

mcqs.q: Is the internal energy of a system the same as the heat it contains?
options: Light must go from a less dense to a denser medium.
Yes — internal energy is just the stored heat in the object.
No — a system doesn't 'contain heat'; internal energy is the total kinetic and potential energy of its particles, changed by heating or doing work.
No — internal energy refers only to the chemical potential energy.
